title: Production debugging — owning problems end-to-end
exp: This is the most under-prepared topic at 4 YOE. Interviewers want to know if you own problems or defer. Prepare one real production incident story — a SCIM provisioning failure or evidence pipeline timeout qualifies.
pts: **Structured approach:** check logs/metrics → narrow scope (which service? which request type?) → form a specific hypothesis → verify with targeted logging → fix → verify metric returned to baseline
**SQL deadlock:** Extended Events or sys.dm_tran_locks. Read deadlock graph to identify two competing transactions. Fix: consistent lock-acquisition order or READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT isolation

**.NET memory leak causes:** static event subscriptions (publisher holds reference to subscriber), undisposed IDisposable, large long-lived caches with no eviction policy, closures capturing large objects
**Your SCIM story:** if a user provisioning event failed silently — how did you detect it? What telemetry did you add? How did you verify the fix?

qa.q: Walk me through debugging a production issue you can't reproduce locally.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) Check logs and metrics around the time the issue started — look for error spikes, latency changes. 2) Narrow scope: which endpoint? Which users? Which data pattern? 3) Form a specific hypothesis. 4) Verify with targeted logging or a feature flag, not a full redeploy. 5) Fix, deploy, watch the metric. 6) Add a permanent alert so you detect this category faster next time.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Requires understanding the underlying execution engine mechanics, memory layout, and runtime optimization pathways for Production debugging — owning problems end-to-end.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Under high concurrency or large data volume, misconfiguring or misusing Walk can trigger CPU spikes, memory leaks, or execution bottlenecks.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Balancing execution performance, maintainability, and operational complexity requires explicit architectural evaluation before adoption.

qa.q: What are the most common causes of memory leaks in a long-running .NET service?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) Static event subscriptions — publisher holds a reference to subscriber, preventing GC. 2) Undisposed IDisposable objects — especially DbContext or HttpClient misuse. 3) Unbounded caches — MemoryCache entries with no eviction policy grow indefinitely. 4) Closures capturing large objects in long-lived delegates. Fix: explicit disposal patterns, IMemoryCache with size limits, weak references where appropriate.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: How do you debug a SQL deadlock in production SQL Server?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Enable deadlock trace or Extended Events. Wait for the next deadlock — SQL Server logs a deadlock graph to the error log or XE target. Read the graph: it shows Transaction A, Transaction B, the resources each holds, and what each is waiting for. Fix: ensure all code that touches both tables acquires locks in the same order, or enable READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT ISOLATION on the database to use row versioning instead of locks.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.
